prompt.context: The state of California has experienced devastating wildfires in recent years, causing deaths and billions of dollars worth of damage. The disasters are only projected to intensify, and the government needs to act fast. The governor has hired you to propose an action plan for prevention and mitigation.
prompt.question: What factors would you analyse to develop an action plan for preventing and mitigating California wildfires?

clarifying_info.q: What is the primary objective — saving lives, minimizing property damage, or both?
clarifying_info.a: Both, but focus on a holistic action plan covering prevention and mitigation.

clarifying_info.q: Are there budget constraints for the proposed solutions?
clarifying_info.a: Not specified; consider feasibility and cost as part of your analysis.

clarifying_info.q: Is the focus on the entire state or specific regions?
clarifying_info.a: Statewide, though certain geographies may be prioritized based on risk.

exhibits.title: California Historical Wildfire Report
exhibits.shows: Bar charts showing Number of Fires by Source (Utilities Failure, Human Error, Natural Causes) and Total Area Burned by Source (Thousand Acres) for years 2000, 2010, and 2020.

exhibits.title: 2022 California Department of Forestry Analysis
exhibits.shows: A table comparing three cities (Oakland, Santa Barbara, Sacramento) across cost to build SafeWall, number of residential structures, % of structures at-risk, annual wildfires, % that are catastrophic, and average property value. Notes: SafeWall reduces probability of catastrophic fire by 50%; catastrophic defined as destroying 10% of at-risk structures.

framework: Diagnosing the Crisis: Causes of Fire (utilities failure, human error, natural causes), Geographic Spread, Trends Over Time — identify which causes are more prevalent and preventable
Action Measures — Prevention: current prevention methods, addressable gaps, categorized by time horizon (short-term quick fixes vs. long-term infrastructure changes)
Action Measures — Response: current response tactics, new or existing tactics to implement, effectiveness of various strategies
Feasibility: Financial Cost of proposed solutions, Legal and Regulatory barriers (lawmakers, utility companies, private sector), Ability to Implement given scale

questions.prompt: Hand the candidate Exhibit 1 when they discuss causes or trends. What insights can they draw from the historical wildfire data?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) Human error fires have doubled over 20 years (1,200 to 6,400) while other causes are relatively constant — this is an avoidable cause and a focus area for prevention policy. (2) Acres burned from human error also steadily increased, but remain relatively smaller in magnitude per fire — suggesting frequent, smaller fires. (3) Outlier years: 2010 shows a spike in natural causes area burned (~270K acres) and 2020 shows a spike in utilities failure area burned (~220K acres) — likely single disaster fires inflating the year. These are harder to prevent short-term but candidates should suggest long-term mitigation measures.

questions.prompt: An environmental minister has suggested building a fireproof structure called SafeWall around one city to reduce the probability of a catastrophic wildfire by 50%. Using Exhibit 2, which city should receive SafeWall and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should systematically calculate expected value saved for each city using three steps. Santa Barbara yields the highest value saved (~$1.125B), roughly 5x that of Oakland or Sacramento. Candidate should note construction costs are similar across cities (~$5.8-7.0M) and are not a differentiating factor. Candidate should also note that more population data would be needed to evaluate purely on humanitarian grounds.

math.setup: Step 1: Total At-Risk Value ($B) = Residential Structures × % At Risk × Avg Property Value ($M) / 1000. Step 2: Expected Catastrophic Fires = Annual Wildfires × % that are Catastrophic. Step 3: Expected Cost No SafeWall ($M) = Total At-Risk Value ($B) × 1000 × Expected Catastrophic Fires × 10% destruction. Value Saved ($M) = Expected Cost No SafeWall × 50% (SafeWall reduction).
steps: Santa Barbara Expected Cost No SafeWall: $10.0B × 2.25 × 10% = $2,250M
math.answer: Santa Barbara saves the most value at $1,125M (~$1.1B), approximately 5x the value saved in Oakland ($200M) or Sacramento ($225M). Recommend building SafeWall around Santa Barbara.

brainstorming.prompt: Given the open-ended nature of the problem, brainstorm ideas across causes, prevention, and response tactics.

categories.name: Human Error Prevention
ideas: Ban or restrict campfire use in high-risk seasons and areas
Anti-littering and cigarette disposal awareness campaigns
Penalties and enforcement for careless fire-starting activities
Regulate gender reveal events and similar activities with open flames

categories.name: Utilities Failure Prevention
ideas: Update and reinforce high-risk power lines in fire-prone zones
Require underground cabling in highest-risk corridors
Collaborate with utility companies on risk-sharing and compliance

categories.name: Natural Causes Mitigation
ideas: Long-term forest management to reduce dry fuel load
Clear firebreaks in forests to contain spread
Prescribed burns to manage vegetation during low-risk windows

categories.name: Short-Term Response Tactics
ideas: Station more firefighters in high-risk areas during fire season
Purchase additional water-planes and aerial assets
Deploy rapid-response teams with better coordination
Improve early warning and evacuation systems

categories.name: Long-Term Infrastructure
ideas: Build SafeWall or equivalent fireproof barriers around at-risk urban areas
Implement drone detection fleet for early fire identification
Invest in weather and fire-spread modeling systems
Develop statewide fireproof zoning standards for new construction

recommendation: Based on data trends, action should be prioritized to reduce wildfires caused by human error, as these have doubled over 20 years and represent a preventable and growing threat
Long-term solutions should also be implemented to mitigate high-damage disaster fires caused by utilities failures and natural causes
Building SafeWall around Santa Barbara is recommended as it is expected to save over $1B in real estate value — approximately 5x the benefit of building it around Oakland or Sacramento
risks: Effectiveness of prevention measures is uncertain and difficult to measure in the short term
High financial cost of long-term infrastructure changes may face budget constraints
Legal and regulatory barriers from utility companies, private sector, and lawmakers may slow implementation
Climate change may intensify fire conditions faster than interventions can scale
next_steps: Short-term: station additional firefighters in high-risk zones, purchase water-planes, ban campfires in fire season
Short-term: launch public awareness campaigns targeting human error sources
Long-term: update high-risk power lines, clear forest firebreaks, implement drone detection fleet
Long-term: begin SafeWall construction around Santa Barbara; evaluate expansion to other cities based on updated risk data
Commission further studies on population density and humanitarian impact to complement the property-value analysis
